actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This snake is very widespread in sub-Saharan Africa, ranging from Senegal in the west to East Africa (north to Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia - Largen 1997), and south to South Africa (Trape and Mané 2006). In West Africa it has been reported from Senegal, the Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Cöte d'Ivoire, Ghana, southern Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria and Cameroon (Trape and Mané 2006), and also ranges into northern Sierra Leone and Liberia. It is also widespread in Togo, where it occurs as far north as Aledjo but may extend to the Sudanese savannah of the country's far north (Segniagbeto et al. 2011). It occurs from sea level to 2,400 m asl in Ethiopia (Largen and Rasmussen 1993), although in East Africa it appears to be absent above 2,200 m asl (Spawls et al. 2002). The paucity of records from northern Kenya, western Tanzania and much of Ethiopia is probably an artefact of under-recording of this cryptic snake (Largen and Rasmussen 1993, Spawls et al. 2002). A number of records exist for South Sudan (Loveridge 1955).
documentation.population: This snake is relatively common in some areas but rare in others. Its population is thought to be stable.
documentation.habitats: This is a diurnal, almost wholly arboreal snake of open forest and savanna (from moist savanna to semi-desert - Spawls et al. 2002). It is particularly associated with savanna woodland and thornbush (Largen and Rasmussen 1993) and usually absent from high grassland and dense forest (Spawls et al. 2002). This fast-moving snake preys on arboreal lizards, including chameleons and agamas as well as smaller lizards (Trape and Mané 2006), but will also take rodents, frogs, nestlings and bird eggs (Spawls et al. 2002). Females lay 8 to 25 eggs in warm, moist microhabitats such as deep holes or damp tree hollows (Spawls et al. 2002). Incubation time is 3–4 months in East Africa (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.threats: There are no major threats to this very widespread snake.
documentation.measures: It is unlikely that any specific conservation measures are required for this species. The Boomslang occurs in Yankari National Park in Nigeria and Mole National Park in Ghana; it is certain that this very wide-ranging snake occurs within more protected areas than is currently known. Taxonomic research is underway into the systematics of this likely species complex.
documentation.use_trade: There is some trade from Tanzania, with a current export quota of 200 animals (J. Beraducci pers. comm. 2014). It is not likely that the species is exported in these numbers, as it is dangerous and difficult to keep. Jensen et al. (2018) found that, although the species commands high prices from private sellers, between 2013 and 2017 only 61 animals were recorded in trade from Tanzania, Uganda, Cameroon and Togo combined.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern because the Boomslang has a very wide distribution and an apparently stable population, and is subject to no major threats.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Dispholidus is presently considered to be a monotypic genus, however the complex pattern of regional morphological variation in this very widespread snake has led to suggestions that the species is a complex (summarized by Eimermacher 2012). On the basis of molecular evidence, this author identified four clades within D. typus that are likely to warrant recognition at specific status. Formal descriptions based on these results and on morphological data are in preparation, and additional cryptic species may be found within the D. typus complex (Eimermacher 2012). Broadley and Blaylock (2013) considered populations in (mainly) the Western and Eastern Cape provinces as being referable to D. t. typus, while populations elsewhere in the range (where males are usually mainly green dorsally) were treated as D. t. viridis.
